title: The family word jar: one bilingual word a day from an empty kitchen jar
description: An empty jar and scraps of paper: each evening someone adds one word in two languages, and each morning your child pulls one out to use during the day.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: The family word jar: one bilingual word a day from an empty kitchen jar
body:
Most households have an empty jar somewhere in a cupboard. That jar can hold a small, growing collection of words your family actually uses — chosen by you, not by a worksheet.

Setup takes five minutes. Rinse the jar, tear some paper into strips (junk mail works), and leave a pen next to it. That is the whole kit.

Each evening, one person adds one word. Write it in both languages, with the language you are building on top: if you are building Spanish, "el paraguas" on top and "umbrella" underneath; if you are building English, "umbrella" on top and "el paraguas" underneath. Pick a word that came up that day — something your child asked about, pointed at, or needed and did not have. Those are the words worth keeping.

Each morning, your child pulls out one strip without looking. That is the word of the day. The job is to use it once before dinner, in any sentence, even if the rest of the sentence is in the other language: "¿Dónde está el paraguas?" or "where's my umbrella?". Anyone in the family can use it too, and spotting when someone does is half the fun.

At dinner, ask who used the word. No points, no prize — just a moment to say it once more.

Then the strip goes back in the jar. Words come back around at random, which is exactly what you want: a word pulled three times in a month gets used three times.

A few rules keep the jar working. Children can add words too, and they should: a child who chose a word is already interested in it. Keep words concrete at first — things, actions, colours — and leave the abstract ones for later. And when the jar gets crowded, take out the words everyone uses easily and move them to a second jar labelled "we know these". Watching that second jar fill up is a record your child can see, with no chart and no test.

If your child cannot read yet, draw the word instead of writing it, or let them draw it. The drawing is the reminder; you say the word aloud when they pull it out.
